en: Prosperity!
May the illustrious Śrīnivāsa be ever victorious!
The Life of the Great Mahāmahopādhyāya, the Lion among Scholars, the Emperor of Grammarians, the Illustrious Śrī Subbarāyācārya Mahāśaya,
whose feet are praised by the foremost deities such as the Lord of Śrī Veṅkaṭagiri and the Source of the Vedas (Brahmā).
I worship the Lord of Śrī, the stainless one, who possesses infinite knowledge, bliss, and other [attributes], as my refuge.
[This is] the work of the venerable Subbarāyācārya of Śrīmuṣṇa, who is highly praised by the best of scholars,
and whose partial majesty has been manifested by the title "Vidvatkesari" (Lion among the Learned).

Having taken from that ocean of jewels—the multitude of virtues—just a few gems, I fashion this necklace to adorn the necks of the virtuous; for whom shall it be a source of joy? There exists in the land of Bhārata a sacred field (kṣetra) honored by the illustrious Madhvācārya.
On the high cheek of the Yadu lineage, the Makarī-leaf ornament known as Śrīmuṣṇa blazes forth.
There, on the banks of the Nityasarovara lake, where the stairs are polished by the touch of the Lord of the Gods who has been liberated,
Hari shines as a boar for the welfare of his devotees, having removed their ignorance.

There lived one named Nārāyaṇārya, whose virtues were praised by the assembly of noble ones, who was like a pearl upon the crest-jewel of the lineage of noble teachers, and who was beloved by scholars for his auspicious conduct. He had five sons who had attained the right method and were experts in the systems of grammar.
Among them was the eminent scholar Śrī Subbarāya, who had churned the depths of Vedānta and whose mind was like a bee at the lotus feet of Hari; he was like Arjuna among the Pāṇḍavas,
born as if from the ocean of Ambā, whose womb was filled with the waters of his own meritorious deeds, just as the moon arises from the great sea.
Within just two or three years brought by his parents, he acquired the true sciences;
staying in his maternal uncle’s house in the village of Tiruvālūr, he studied the Rigvedic hymns.
Having studied the works of Kāvyā from his father, his elder brother, the intelligent youth [mastered them].
In that field of Manāruguḍi, where the divine Lord Śrī Vārṣṇeya shines together with Rukmiṇī, the wise man resided, honored by all learned scholars;
and from that preeminent scholar there, named Gopālācārya, [the teaching] was received by the steadfast one.
Then, having mastered the Śābda-tantra, the Kaustubha, and the Kaumudī under his teacher—
who had bestowed upon him the blessing, "You shall become proficient in the scriptures"—
he took as his wife a maiden of faultless limbs, who was well-disposed toward him and of auspicious conduct.
Later, while wandering in the northern region, he reached the city of Surapura.
Having skillfully studied several treatises, such as the *Śekhara*, under the noble and eminent scholar Hayagrīva, and having received his permission, he proceeded to the region north of that place.
And where, on the Bhīmākūla bank, the supreme Hari named Viṭṭhala reigns victorious;
from there, with devotion, he reached that excellent sacred field named Paṇḍharapura.
There, indeed, the wise man took refuge in Kṛṣṇācārya, the foremost among the learned.
Having thoroughly studied the *Bhāṣya* along with the *Pradīpa*, as well as the *Bhūṣaṇasāra*, the *Mañjūṣā*, and the *Uddyota*,
he became a man of great wisdom in the science of grammar (*śābda-tantra*). Observing the excellence of his learning and his eloquence, the venerable teacher [was impressed].
"You shall be honored in all assemblies by those headed by kings"—
having spoken this blessing, he accepted it with a prostration.
And he, walking on foot, bestowed the estate of Kolhāpura upon his disciples.
For in that city, where Lakṣmī dwells, bestowing all desired objects upon her devotees,
he resided and studied the entire science of Nyāya from the illustrious Bhikṣu Śāstrivarya,
a crest-jewel among the crown gems of the assembly of scholars. (19-20)
In that very city, he defeated the logician named Raghunātha,
who had composed a commentary on the *Pañcavāda* titled *Nyāyaratna*.
That eloquent man brought supreme joy to the scholars residing there.
Returning to his own country, he gradually reached the city of Mysore.
There, in the royal assembly, he won the high honor of the king from among the learned scholars;
O King, [this was] under the ruler of the city named New Durga in the southern region.
From the learned Kuppusvāmī Śāstrin,

who was like the moon risen from the milk-ocean of his own lineage and whose intellect was praised by the lords of scholars, [he] first obtained the Pūrvamīmāṃsā; he who taught the true meaning of the scriptures of Śrī Pūrṇaprajña to excellent disciples.
Many times, from that preeminent teacher named Rāmaṇṇācārya— a treasure-house of excellent qualities—
this [author] studied for a long time until he reached the end of the traditional transmission (āmnāya) on the shore of the western ocean,
in the city known as Śrī-Rajatapīṭha.

From the illustrious Yatikulatilaka, the preeminent worshipper of Kṛṣṇa honored by the sage Śrī Pūrṇaprajña and others, he received the sacred initiation (dīkṣā). He received it from that sun among masters of knowledge, who had dispelled the darkness [of ignorance] through his disciples.

Thus, by the power of his incomparable intellect and eloquence, this lion among scholars wandered through various regions, always disregarding even the best of learned men who were like elephants of the quarters. Yet, in a certain excellent village, he shared a seat with them in a great assembly.
Then, in a debate at the court of the King of Tanjore, the examiner of scholars, Budharāja Śāstrin, defeated him and other learned men; yet,
although he knew him to be proficient in the investigation of the scriptures, he did not [challenge] him in the first round.
Then, becoming enraged in the midst of the assembly before the Lord, he declared:
"In this council of scholars, who is capable of examining me or providing answers to my questions? (31-32)
Then the wise man, having been questioned by the Lord as to what this was, replied in fear:
"This is a mere accidental offense on my part; it deserves my first salutation.
Thus he spoke his first salutation, saying, "There is no doubt."
All the worlds were struck with wonder and attained immeasurable joy.
Then, on one occasion at that very place, many scholars from the southern region,
having deliberated together, challenged the highly eminent Kuppu-swāmī-ayyaṅgār in the assembly.
They urged this exceedingly wise man to conquer the king of logicians;
he defeated him in debates within the treatise named *Vyutpattivāda*.
Then, all the noble-minded scholars there [honored] the victorious Subbarāyācārya.
Considering him to be no other than the preceptor of the gods, the learned addressed him as a universal emperor (cakravartin).
By him alone, the unprecedented science of grammar was firmly established in the southern quarter, just as the Ganges, rendered exceedingly pure by Bhagiratha, first brought the earth.
In whichever regions there currently shine those most renowned,
victorious scholars of the court and assembly who have reached the further shore of the science of grammar (vyākaraṇa)—
honored for their celebrated intellects in debates and in correct instruction— 39.
And they bear the title of Mahāmahopādhyāya, bestowed by King Jārji.
In the preeminent royal halls, these scholars shine resplendently;
all of them are lords among the wise, [each being] a teacher of disciples, grand-disciples, and their own students within the scriptures.
In this way, other learned men also dwell in the systems of Jaimini and Gautama;
who is able to describe the great fortune of these many others?
[This occurs] in the city of Rājamahendra, in the assembly of the venerable teacher Satyadhyānatīrtha.
There, the great elephant among grammarians, intoxicated with pride, arrived amidst the wise who were like elephants.
Beholding this lion among scholars summoned by the eminent Guru, that disputant quickly put all others to flight with the blows of his tusks—those difficult-to-parry challenges. (43–44)
Terrified, he bowed to the best of scholars and spoke in the midst of the assembly:
"Which disputant would be capable of engaging in debate with these venerable masters?
They are the great ones in this world—Pāṇini, or Patañjali, or even Brahmī."
"In this assembly, I have today been defeated by these eminent scholars.
46 Just as the wise Pārtha alone swiftly conquered all the Saṃśaptakas, so too Bhīma alone, through the power of his intellect, has vanquished these lords of debate like the Krodhavaśas. 47
Having himself sought out and summoned the most eminent, renowned, arrogant, and fierce scholars—
whose pride had been shattered— he, firm of intellect, made them take an oath without hesitation.
He hurls the terrifying *śataghnī* weapon into the ranks of the great chariot-warriors among the lords of wicked disputants.
He quickly released a thousand-slaying arrow in the form of an invincible challenge;
then, having been summoned again by the ministers in the city of Maisūra,
that king defeated the learned men there and obtained the position of examiner bestowed upon him.
Having examined the scholars who had come from many lands, he satisfied the king;
this king of the learned was highly honored by the royal ministers in the presence of the wise.
In the assembly of the King of Baroda, he [defeated] all those lions among scholars, the very ornaments of the assembly.

Having conquered in all the sciences, he obtained the highest honor as a foremost scholar. He shone in the Kerala country on the shore of the southern ocean, where the darkness was dispelled by the light of the toe-nail of the lotus-foot of Śrī Padmanābha.
In the city of Anantaśayana, having defeated the learned disputants in the royal assembly,
he received the highest and first honor, consisting of golden bracelets and armlets.
He shone in the sacred field of Padmavatīvara near the glorious Veṅkaṭagiri mountain.
In that excellent assembly, which upholds the principles of the venerable Pūrṇaprajña,
is convened by virtuous men, proclaims the established tenets, and is graced by the foremost of the wise—
within that circle of eminent scholars, he first adorned the position of examiner.
Having observed his skillful compositions with great delight, Cittūru Kalekaṭaragrya finally rejoiced in this master’s treatises, beginning with the *Sūtrārthamañjarī*.
Having personally presented them to the king, preceded by an expression of his own intention—
The illustrious Emperor Shri George bestowed upon him the most highly honored title of "Mahāmahopādhyāya" as a reward for his annual tribute;
he then sent word from the city of Delhi that this name had been conferred.
He whose intellect dispels the darkness [of ignorance] by roaming to the very depths of the ocean of the treatises on logic and grammar,
and whom Lakṣmī and Sarasvatī have affectionately sought out with intense rivalry;
before whom even all those known as "wise" (budha) fear to utter his name.

The King of the Koṅkaṇa country, whose excellent fame was being celebrated by poets and storytellers, beheld his [the author's] genius regarding difficult and complex problems that were otherwise impossible to solve;
with a mind struck with wonder and filled with joy, he bestowed upon him golden bracelets and other gifts. (61–62)
In Vārāṇasī, within the assembly for the debate of scholars, all those of great intellect,
recognizing his matchless and previously unknown sinless mastery of the ocean of grammatical science,
were submerged in a sea of wonderful joy and bestowed upon him a name truly worthy of its meaning.
Having honored the title "Lion among Grammarians" in the assembly of the best of the wise,
there [in that city] dwells Hara, who bears the name "I am the remover of the distress of those who bow before me," rejoicing together with Śivā, known by the name Dharmāsaṃvardhinī.
In the sacred field of Pañcanada, where the dust of sins was swept away by the waters and breezes of the Kāverī,
he dwelt teaching his circle of disciples the entirety of the scriptures without ceasing.
His son, a learned man of auspicious conduct known as Setumādhava, [followed in his footsteps].
In the renowned and excellent sacred field named Tirupati, the blissful abode of the Lord of Śrī,
at the Śrī Veṅkaṭeśa Sanskrit College which has long flourished,
the intelligent [Vīrarāghava] attained the position of chief instructor in the system of Pāṇini. (67–68)
In the sacred valley at the foot of the mountain named Śrī Veṅkaṭa,
together with his beloved son, this wise man resided in Tirupati, which shines with purity.
There, for a long time, he himself [taught] many scriptures to his disciples.
By teaching, he satisfied Acyuta Muni, and by constantly honoring him, he pleased the lords of the sages.
This cluster of jewels consisting of the meaning of the Sūtras, composed by that lord of scholars, has been sealed by his son; it is honored by all with both their heads and their hearts.
He has also composed two excellent commentaries on the pair of commentaries known as the *Śekhara* on the *Gītā-bhāṣya*;
these have now been placed for printing by his son.
(72) There dwell in various lands many disciples and groups of grand-disciples.
Today we are unable to specifically know or state their names.
Now, however, I shall mention the names of a few among those learned men:
the superintendent of the royal Sanskrit school in Pañcanada, who is proficient in grammar (śabda). || 73–74 ||
Born on the banks of the Mahitā river, possessed of excellent qualities praised by his disciples and preceptors,
this Śrī Setumādhavārya was the foremost disciple among them;
he was a scholar who mastered the *Ghanapāṭha*, a master of a hundred simultaneous mental retentions (*śatāvadhānī*), and a most wonderful and eminent poet.
Born of the lineage of Kadalīkanda, he was the teacher Lakṣmaṇācārya, who composed the Gītā-upanyāsa.
His principal disciple was Medhāvī, who likewise studied the entire scripture of grammar (śābda) under him, as well as the Vedānta and the Tantras.
There, in the sacred field of Cidambaram, reside many schools of learning, where the eminent scholar Gopālaśāstrin—a preeminent paṇḍita learned in the system of Pāṇini—dwells;
and there the two gods, Nātha and Vṛṣākapāyin, who bestow boons, reign victorious.
(78) There, in the sacred field of Cidambaram, reside many schools of learning.
He was appointed to the position of the first teacher at the principal school. (79) Consequently, there were many students who had mastered the system of Pāṇini;
among them was a preeminent scholar, the learned Śrī Daṇḍapāṇi Yajvan. (80)
There dwells the foremost of the wise, a scholar of all branches of knowledge and the arts,
who bears the title of Mahāmahopādhyāya in Cidambaram.
That learned man, along with his students and circle of disciples, indeed belongs to this Kulapati.
He who is the preeminent scholar of the Anantaśayana Sanskrit College,
Śrī Rāmakṛṣṇa Śāstrī, is also a disciple of this Bodhakalpataru;
he resides in Kumbhaghoṇa and is known as the modern Bhaṭṭabāṇa.
In the royal hall shining in the excellent city of Kumbhaghōṇa, there was a learned man bearing the title of Mahāmahopādhyāya, the ornament of the family of great poets;
he too was a grammarian, namely Kṛṣṇācārya, who was indeed his very own disciple. (84)
He who was the illustrious Mahāmahopādhyāya, the eminent scholar Vī. Śrīnivāsa Bhaṭṭāraka;

his distinguished disciple was Josaphat Kālejivar, the teacher of the immortal language (Sanskrit) in the most delightful city of Triśiraḥ, in the region surrounding the sacred field of Śrīraṅga. 85–86.

Furthermore, Vāmanabhaṭṭa, surnamed Jhalakīkara, who was an expert in the refined language of the royal court in the city of Punā, the author of a commentary on the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, and a knower of the principles of the science of poetics— was indeed his disciple. (87)
In Solāpur, his learned disciple Govinda Śāstrī was also wise.
(88) This example has been cited, but it is not an exhaustive enumeration of the teacher and his disciples;
many learned logicians acquired the *Vyutpattivāda* from him. (89)

"I too am but a certain disciple; thus I speak, yet I feel ashamed. However, my inclusion among the ranks should be understood as being solely due to the desire for the compassion of the most excellent Guru.
Thus spending his time solely in the practice of discussing the Vedānta scriptures, he remained.
In the Śaka era of Śālivāhana, numbered by the planets (nine), the fires (three), the Vasus (eight), and the moon (one)— that is, 1839—
on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kārttika in the year known as Śrīkālayukti,
this [temple] was fully completed at Tirupati-nagara by means of a form arising from a mass of merit.
"Recollection of him pacifies all evils; he is the cause of all auspicious things for everyone"—thus, impelled by devotion, I have spoken somewhat regarding the greatness of my Guru.
[This was composed] at the Śrī Veṅkaṭeśa Vidyāśālā in the illustrious city of Śrīpade.
The son of the most learned scholar Śrīnivāsa, who was a teacher of the three Vedas (Trayyantopādhyāya),
and Giridhara, born of the Kadalīkanda lineage and a connoisseur of poetics (Sāhitīvidvān),
having composed this virtuous work and offered it to his preceptor, bows down to that most excellent teacher. || 94–95 ||
May the Lord of Rama, the ocean of the waters of compassion, who dwells on the glorious Veṅkaṭagiri, together with Padmāvatī, be pleased with me and grant me what is dear and auspicious.
[In the Śaka year] numbered by the sky (0), the seasons (6), the Vasus (8), and the moon (1)— that is, 1860— of the Śālīvāhana era...
This composition, which extols the venerable Ācāryas, was composed on the full moon day of Caitra in the year Bahudhanya;
it is the work of Śrīpūrṇabodha, who is honored as one who has attained a second birth. || 97 ||

I praise Subbarāyārya, who was born into that very lineage and is highly esteemed; he whose feet were served by countless foremost disciples as well as wise householders, who was a noble teacher of excellent conduct, a renowned preceptor, and an expounder of scriptures not heard before. ||1||

Having constantly acquired the knowledge of the Vedānta from the eminent teacher Rāmaṇṇācārya— whose name is renowned for his commentaries and who possesses a collection of treatises on the arts of the noble wind (grammar)— and having likewise learned its meaning;
[he is] a yogin who, bowing to the lords of yogins at the Kṛṣṇāpura monastery, shines with the rays of sacred knowledge.
I praise Subbarāyārya, who, obstructing the darkness within, has become the preceptor of all virtuous people. ||2||
By him alone was produced here on earth this great, pure, and preeminent knowledge of grammar, like the celestial river (Ganges), complete, delightful in its practice, and entirely unprecedented;
for all these lords among scholars have been satisfied by drinking even a few drops of it again and again.
I perpetually praise Subbarāyārya, the most excellent of gurus, from whom [I] have obtained knowledge, like a divine river. ||3||
Wherever and however many there may be who are called the most excellent of gods through their verbal knowledge—
all these,
too, are manifestly [the fruits] of the very same well-sown seeds known as clear and radiant instructions that have fully grown.
I praise the noble Subbarāya, who is honored as being born from Him for some, yet born from another for others. ||4||

In the assembly hall of King Yashadāsa at Tanjāpur, he was presented with the first debate, worthy of the judges; when it was said, "At this time of examination, you ought not to remain here today," he then defeated even those wise elephants among scholars in all the scriptures.
I praise Subbarāyārya, whose intellect is firm and incomparable, who remained right there upon that very seat. ||5||

Whose intellect, which quells the pride of the wise, was such that even one proficient in all the sciences did not come for debate upon hearing of it; yet, when the King of Māyī was once forcibly defeated by him,
another expert in the arena of logic likewise became overwhelmed by excessive fear.
He gave no reply in the *Vyutpattivāda*; oh, I praise the noble Subbarāya! ||6||

Having heard of the wisdom and fame of Śrī George Chakravarti— which was praised by all the learned and renowned throughout every land— the King, his mind exceedingly delighted, honored him properly, bestowing upon him ornaments,
fine armor and other gifts, and a meaningful title, along with silver coins.
Year after year, I praise the noble Subbarāya, who is devoted to the feet of the Lord of Śrī for a hundred years. ||7||

In the assembly of the venerable Satyajñānatīrtha, the foremost of ascetics, he— who was a formidable lion among great debaters— struck down with the forceful blows of his tusks the arrogant elephant of a learned scholar who had arrived there;
he shattered that elephant, which cast other wise men far away, by breaking it with the great spears of his rejoinders.
I praise Subbarāya Ārya, whose awakening is like instantaneous lightning and who is the destroyer of adversaries. 8.

This Mañjarī, which has been bound together by one who is highly purified and skilled in the art of concise and expansive exposition, and which is perfectly suited for the instruction of both the learned with sharp intellects and children;

this peerless work, its slender body radiant with the jewels of the meaning of the Sūtras, attains the reputation of being an ear-ornament for wise men who delight in the words of the Sūtra and Bhāṣya. (9)
While that lion among scholars roamed within the forest of the king’s assembly of eminent men, the elephants known as grammarians, utterly terrified, did not utter even a single sound;
and the herds of leopards known as logicians, though possessing the cruel fangs of fallacious reasoning, were rendered helpless by fear.
The multitudes of serpents among the tantrikas remained hidden somewhere, not even uttering a loud sound. ||10||
Though there were other beloved ones, he alone was granted incomparable and constant affection;
by him, the lord of debaters, the various great defeats inflicted by the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra were avoided;
and by that foremost of heroes, the science of the Madhva doctrine was made to flourish incessantly.
May that noble Bhīma, like the Pāñcālī in his own treatise, bestow excellent understanding upon Subbarāya. 11.

There existed the form of the moon-crested Lord (Śiva), which was worthy of being sought by the noble, pure, untainted, and named Indumauli; it was praised by the universe, the bestower of all desired objects, yet difficult to attain.
For the sake of making that [form] easily known to supplicants, and out of compassion for others, [this work is composed] for their great joy.
It is said that he composed the beautiful commentary named *Subodhinī*, which possesses the luster of divine collyrium.
In this world, from the eastern ocean to the Himalayas, there was no scholar whom he had not defeated in debates;
nor was there any wise man anywhere who, when overwhelmed by a flood of refutations employed by scholars driven by intense persistence,
felt agitation, anxiety, mental distress, or even negligence.
The series of replies emerging from the mouth of that mountain was like the river of the Sun (the Yamunā) flowing forth from Mount Meru.

In his own city named Śrīpada, he— who was yearning to behold the pair of lotus feet of the glorious Lord of Śeṣācala— joyfully provided with food and abundant comforts, preceded by oil massages, those foremost of the twice-born who had arrived there weary, accompanied by their sons and wives, treating them with great respect.
I praise Subbarāya Ārya, who was teaching the science of prosody to his son, the most excellent among the learned. ||14||
For from this mountain-like work, which possesses many excellent deeds, divine rivers have issued forth;
by reading it even once or bathing in them, they destroy all mental afflictions of the virtuous and uproot the lofty trees of pride grown in the minds of rival disputants.
May that which is remembered bestow auspiciousness upon us—[the work] of the illustrious and renowned preceptor Subbarāya. 15.
Thus, the poet Giridhara, whose mind is fixed upon the lotus feet of the venerable teacher Subbarāyottama, who is born of the lineage of Mocākanda and is the son of Śrīnivāsārya,
having taken up a few choice pearls from the virtues of that boundless ocean of merit—
Therefore, may the Guru place this garland upon my own neck, bestowing upon me right understanding. ||16||
Victory to Śrī Śrīnivāsa,
the Great Mahopādhyāya, the Sun of Knowledge, the Ornament of the Madhva Siddhānta, and the venerable Muṣṇa Vyākaraṇa.

Victorious is the noble birth of the venerable Guru, who shines like a pearl, born into the lineage of the preceptors named Āryācārya— who are served by wise householders who are the best of swans, and whose pure souls are submerged in an ocean of excessive joy arising from the direct perception of the charming horse-faced [Hayagrīva], adorned with a multitude of flowers that are the blue-lotus glances from the corner of Lakṣmī’s eyes. (1)
Victorious is that irreproachable verbal science which, rising daily from the mountain of her mouth,
effortlessly and swiftly dispels even the darkness residing within the hearts of the multitude of disciples;
and which, constantly illuminating the eternally pure and vast abode of Viṣṇu, ever triumphs.
He shines even today, irresistible like the scorching rays of the sun; I praise that glorious Guru. ||2||
"Ah, there are indeed more than a hundred wise men upon this earth, yet they are not truly well-born;
there are others who are unwise though born of great lineages"—such is the thought in the minds of the virtuous.
For today there is great sorrow regarding him who was born of an excellent family and is the foremost among the wise.
As soon as he was seen, he departed from me; may that teacher, who is worthy of universal acclaim, be victorious. ||3||

Noble lineage, pure wisdom through mastery of the scriptures, the ability to teach, practice of the true Dharma, compassion, forbearance, tranquility, self-control, splendor, beauty, devotion, and other such virtues shine together in mutual harmony—oh, may that very teacher, my treasury of qualities who has attained such great friendship with them, bestow prosperity upon me every day. (4)

Scholarship indeed may generally be acquired by men through great effort, yet noble birth can never be attained even by the most intense exertions. Just as fragrance is not found in a golden lotus, so too true learning does not reside in one who lacks noble lineage; this saying shines forth, and having encountered such a person, we bow to him with reverence. (5)
Drinking again and again the nectar-stream of the commentary on the lineage of the most purifying and glorious Āgamas, the disciples are filled with joy like cakora birds;
it is a marvel that they do not cease from drinking what has flowed from his stainless moon-like mouth.
May this king of gurus always be for my thorough understanding of the authentic scriptures. ||6||
The son of the noble preceptor Subbarāya— a lion among scholars, who was like a vast ocean of nectar to the great Ācāryas,
a moon to the sky of the [Vedic] tradition, whose fame resounded through the drums of all the Buddhas, and who was honored by all as a treasury of universal vision—
was a wise man equal to his father.
May the scholar Setumādhava, the foremost among the learned on earth, live forever. ||7||

Born for the joy of the world from the glorious Vijayodara, as the moon rises from the eastern mountain, he was born in the most pure land near the city of Śrī-Tañjānagara, on the bank of the Sahyādrijā (Kāverī), in the auspicious agrahāra known as Pañcanada, which is like a necklace upon the earth.
May my Guru, who constantly satisfies all people with his moonlight-like splendor, be victorious for a long time. ||8||

Having studied all the scriptures under his father’s feet and being honored by scholars, the eminent teacher Padakalopādhyāya—who is an ocean of compassion for his disciples—has finally settled here in the illustrious city of Śrīpadapura, illuminating the excellent Sanskrit college established with funds provided by the venerable Lord Śrī Veṅkaṭeśvara. (9)

For thirty years, he taught at the Vishva Vidyalaya many disciples, providing them with a complete and doubt-free mastery of the great primary treatise, the Mahābhāṣya— the foremost of excellent scriptures— through its secret, infinite, sweet, and radiant connection with the traditional meanings.
That eminent scholar, who himself has crossed over all examinations, reigns here as the sovereign among the great teachers. ||10||

It is a marvel that his son, by whom this incomparable and rare treatise on grammar was composed as a most auspicious silken garment for every limb of the Goddess of Learning under the guidance of his venerable father,
has today likewise adorned the beautiful bodies of the damsels of all the directions.
They were adorned with silken cloths of equal value, highly prized, and spread over many feet. ||11||
For by him indeed this vast hall has attained great loftiness through its well-fashioned pillars;
he who, drawn by the abundance of his virtues, was regarded as a beloved husband even by one who was aged;
and it was out of longing for a connection with him that his sister bestowed her daughter upon his youthful disciple.
May this very Śrī Guru of mine, a mine of jewels of excellent qualities, continuously bestow what is most beneficial. 12.

The Śābdī [Mañjūṣā], exceedingly beautiful with its jewels of ornaments, adorned with a noble crest-jewel, possessing an excellent commentary, its form embraced by the delightful, radiant with the gems of words,
and endowed with the meaning of the Mañjūṣā, vibrates with aesthetic delight within his mouth upon the stage.
Dancing like a joyful actress, she expands the joy of the assembly of seekers of knowledge. ||13||

He who is constantly praised by the most eminent masters of truth and meditation— whose intellects have been sharpened on the whetstone of discerning wisdom and whose golden height of excellence is peerless among the scholars dwelling upon the circle of the earth— and who is honored in every assembly, rejoices.
We pay homage for our own welfare to that preceptor Setumādhava, the best among the learned. ||14||
Having repeatedly recognized his kindness, purity, compassion, self-restraint, proficiency in seeking knowledge, and skill in discerning tasks,
the excellent superintendent of the school made him his own bearer of the burden, and continues to do so.
May this very lord of poets, my guru, grant me skill upon the path of poetry. ||15||
He who constantly gratifies seekers of knowledge with respectful and eloquent words,
guests with sweet foods, the poor with appropriate wealth, and the wise with learning;
and who honors Veṅkaṭapati with devotion and worship through the teachings of the illustrious Madhva-śāstra.
May my preceptor Setumādhava nourish my supreme knowledge of Śrī Vyāsa. 16.

The one named Kalesha, born from the ocean of milk of the lineage called Atreya, a highly intelligent and most excellent scholar bearing the title Śrīmuṣṇa, was born from the venerable Subbarāyārya, who established the true Dharma of the noble Śrīmuṣṇa tradition.
May Acyuta grant to this venerable Guru a lifespan of more than a hundred years. ||17||

Thus, constantly impelled by the excellent qualities that are the objects of the experience of all people, Giridhara, who cherishes them as his own gurus, praises the beloved Śrīpati out of curiosity—
the Lord of Śrī, who dwells in the heart of our teacher and resides within the lotus of the mind of Amitabuddhi.
May he be well-pleased; may he bestow prosperity, longevity, and wisdom upon those who recite this. ||18||
This garland of jewel-like virtues of the venerable Guru Setumādhava has been composed out of curiosity by the poet named Giridhara, born of the lineage of Kadalīkanda. 19.
May this [work], composed by the learned scholar of literature at the Śrī Veṅkaṭeśa Vidyāśālā, the virtuous son of the eminent scholar Śrīnivāsa, long bring auspiciousness to the wise. 20.

Thus was this work composed by Giridharācārya, son of Śrīnivāsācārya and born of the Kadalīkanda lineage, a professor of Sāhitya at the illustrious Veṅkaṭeśvara Saṃskṛta Mahākalāśālā shining in Śrī Padapurī (Tirupati), and one who is proficient in Dvaita Vedānta.
A garland of jewel-like virtues of the Guru.
May this be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
